newsitem.title: USA: Canada frustrated by alleged U.S. salmon overfishing.
newsitem.headline: Canada frustrated by alleged U.S. salmon overfishing.

text.p: Canada's Fisheries Minister on Tuesday voiced mounting frustration over alleged U.S. overfishing of Pacific salmon.

"There is huge frustration in the fishing community (in Canada). Frustration levels are very high," Fisheries and Oceans Minister David Anderson told a news briefing on his arrival for talks with U.S. officials on the controversy.
"We need less of this (U.S.) in your face fishing," he said before meeting U.S. Secretary of Commerce William Daley. "Every Sockeye (salmon) is worth 10 bucks. It's 10 bucks out of their pocket."
Anderson, who is fighting for the rights of Canadian fishermen, also plans to meet senators, U.S. environmental groups and other officials to discuss the bitter dispute.
Canada claims the United States fishing industry is drastically overfishing salmon in violation of the Pacific Salmon Treaty that was signed in 1985.

So-called "salmon interceptions" is at the heart of the dispute, which led to a three-day blockade of the Alaska state ferry Malaspina last week by 200 fishing boats in Prince Rupert, about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) north of Vancouver.

"I want there to be a better understanding of the frustration which has led to these actions...While no one wanted that event there is legitimate cause for a high level of frustration," Anderson said.

The salmon begin their life cycle in fresh water and then migrate to the ocean where they grow and mature before returning to their river of origin to spawn. It is on their return inland to either Washington state and Alaska in the United States or British Columbia in Canada that the fish are caught.

Anderson said since the treaty was signed, U.S. share of Pacific salmon has consistently increased. "U.S. fishermen are deriving substantially greater benefit than is justified by the production in U.S. rivers," he said.
He dismissed U.S. claims that the salmon harvest was bigger this year and that was why U.S. fishermen were yielding more than in previous years.
"Their numbers just don't add up," Anderson said. "We just have not seen the fish they are talking about."
Anderson said the main aims of the 1985 treaty were to ensure equity and conservation of future fishing stocks. Neither of these elements were being adhered to by U.S. fishermen, he said.
"I will not have any fish stocks put in jeopardy just because of a so-called fishing dispute between the United States and Canada," the Canadian minister said.
"The world looks to the United States for leadership on environmental issues and the credibility of the U.S. administration is at risk here," he added.

Last week, both countries appointed special envoys to try and resolve the salmon fishing dispute. William Ruckelshaus, a former Cabinet official, will lead U.S. efforts while University of British Columbia President and Chancellor David Strangway is the Canadian choice.
